Conoce a los peloteros mexicanos que buscan hacer historia en la Serie Mundial de la MLB
Al menos cuatro mexicanos participan en la Serie Mundial de la MLB en este 20226 Joey Ortiz, JoJo Romero, Jonathan Aranda y Manuel Rodríguez.
La Serie Mundial 2026 cuenta con varios mexicanos: Jonathan Aranda, Joey Ortiz y JoJo Romero. Cada uno tiene un papel diferente en sus equipos, pero los tres forman parte de una final que reúne a jugadores vinculados con el beisbol de México.
Los Milwaukee Brewers regresaron a la Serie Mundial después de 44 años. El equipo busca ganar el primer título de su historia con Joey Ortiz en el cuadro interior y JoJo Romero como una de las opciones del bullpen. Por su parte, Jonathan Aranda intenta ayudar a los Tampa Bay Rays a conseguir el campeonato.
Joey Ortiz nació en California y juega como campocorto y tercera base. Durante la temporada regular de 2026, disputó 134 partidos, con un promedio de bateo de .270, nueve jonrones y 47 carreras impulsadas.
La defensa es una de sus principales fortalezas. Joey Ortiz se ha consolidado como una pieza importante para Milwaukee, aunque sus números ofensivos han bajado durante la postemporada.

El jugador también habló sobre Jonathan Aranda, su rival en la Serie Mundial. Joey Ortiz destacó el nivel del primera base de Tampa Bay y se refirió a la oportunidad de competir contra él en el Clásico de Otoño.
JoJo Romero es un lanzador zurdo nacido en Camarillo, California. El relevista llegó a los Brewers en agosto de 2026, después de jugar con los St. Louis Cardinals.

Los partidos, las claves del día y el periódico para hojear — todo en un correo, todos los días. Gratis, y te das de baja con un clic.
Su función es trabajar desde el bullpen en momentos importantes de los partidos. Durante la postemporada, JoJo Romero ha tenido la responsabilidad de frenar a los bateadores rivales en las entradas finales.
Además, JoJo Romero formó parte de la selección mexicana en el Clásico Mundial de Beisbol. El lanzador explicó que sus abuelos siguen sus partidos por televisión y están pendientes de su trayectoria profesional.
Jonathan Aranda, otro de los mexicanos en MLB
Jonathan Aranda integra la lista de mexicanos que participan en la Serie Mundial 2026. El primera base nació en Tijuana y terminó la temporada regular con un promedio de bateo de .274, 22 jonrones y 92 carreras impulsadas.
En el primer partido de la final, Jonathan Aranda conectó tres imparables en tres turnos, recibió una base por bolas y anotó una carrera. Sin embargo, los Rays perdieron por 3-2 ante Milwaukee.
Manuel Rodríguez, nacido en Mérida, Yucatán, también busca un lugar en el Clásico de Otoño. El relevista derecho disputó seis partidos en la temporada regular, en los que registró una efectividad de 2.70 y sumó 10 ponches en seis entradas y dos tercios.
Así, los mexicanos afrontan la Serie Mundial con objetivos distintos. Joey Ortiz y JoJo Romero buscan conquistar el primer campeonato de los Brewers, mientras Jonathan Aranda intenta ayudar a Tampa Bay a levantar el título de las Grandes Ligas.

item.content:encoded:
Welcome to a most fantastically interesting World Series, in which focusing on the size of the markets involved completely misses the forest for the trees. It’s a No. 1-vs.-No. 1 matchup, just the sixth time in the past 30 years that’s happened. It’s a pair of fanbases who have never won before, which marks the first time since 1980 (Royals vs. Phillies) that’s happened, and thus only the second time in more than a century, since the previous time had been 1920.
It’s a matchup of teams that have more than a few connections. Note that Tampa Bay’s top two starters, Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta, each came up with Milwaukee, and were teammates on the 2020-21 Brewers. Note, also, that NLCS MVP Jake Bauers made his debut with Tampa Bay back in 2018, and that Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold spent nine years in the Tampa Bay front office before moving to Wisconsin.
It's more than just that. Depending on how you view your baseball aesthetics, it's a delightfully throwback sort of on-field style. It’s not that these teams eschew analytical thinking -- exactly the opposite, really -- but no team struck out less than the Rays, each team finished in the top five in steals and the bottom 10 in homers, and the bunt hits leaderboard goes “Tampa Bay first, Milwaukee second.”
Throw in a pair of excellent defenses, and you know what you’re going to get here, which is excellent baseball played by a pair of teams that actually look a whole lot like one another. We know what else we're going to get, too: an incredibly interesting series. Which side has the edge?
Catcher
William Contreras, over the past five years, has a pretty solid argument to make as being the best all-around catcher in the National League. While his bat over the last two seasons (110 OPS+) isn’t quite what it was at his peak from 2022-24 (129 OPS+), it’s reliably solid, and then of course he’s been fantastic in eight playoff games, posting a 1.157 OPS with three homers. It’s hard to overstate how important the midseason acquisition of Liam Hicks (129 OPS+ in 41 games for Tampa Bay) was, really helping to lengthen a top-heavy lineup, though he hasn’t done much with the bat in the playoffs. Given relatively similar defensive value, we’ll give a small edge based on track record.
Advantage: Brewers
First base
It's a tale of two winding paths here, as Jonathan Aranda finally had his breakout last season, a decade after he signed as an amateur free agent with Tampa Bay, and of course Jake Bauers' long road to get to this point has been well-chronicled. Bauers has the offensive edge both in terms of power and getting on base, and neither are terribly strong defensive players, so given the mild 2026 regular-season advantage and also the superior performance in October, it’s hard not to choose Bauers on this. Great stories, both.
Advantage: Brewers
Second base
Brice Turang is the best all-around second baseman in the game, pairing excellent defense with a more recently found power stroke, popping 21 homers and driving in 100. The Rays have certainly found some ways to get value out of their second-base duo of Richie Palacios and Ben Williamson, but it’s a relatively below-average spot for Tampa Bay and, either way, we’re comparing to Milwaukee’s best-in-class superstar. This one is probably the biggest mismatch of any pairing on the list.
Advantage: Brewers
Shortstop
Here’s how you know how well-regarded Taylor Walls is on defense: The Rays continue to play him every day despite a near-total lack of offense from the position, as he’s posted all of a .381 OPS this month, and even that was juiced a little by the inexplicable three walks that Cleveland issued him in ALCS Game 6. It’s not just a small-sample thing, either, as Walls has been a routinely ineffective hitter for the entirety of his career.
There’s no doubt that Milwaukee’s Cooper Pratt is a stronger offensive force, though that’s been more good than great, with a league-average line as a rookie and a mostly singles-based approach in the playoffs. While he’s expected to be a quality shortstop as his career progresses, a number of important miscues in the postseason tilt this one to the more surehanded Walls.
Advantage: Rays
Third base
If there’s some argument that this series features more depth than true superstars, then that case falls apart a little at third, where Tampa Bay’s Junior Caminero posted his second consecutive 40-plus homer season on his way to, most likely, some high placement on AL MVP ballots. It’s true that prior to his ALCS Game 6 homer, his bat had been relatively quiet in October, but we’re also talking about all of eight games against some of the best pitching the sport has to offer. (The average fastball he’s seen? 96.8 mph.) There’s an obvious speed-and-defense edge for Milwaukee in David Hamilton and Joey Ortiz, but not quite so much that you’d take either or both over Caminero, or that it’s really close at all.
Advantage: Rays
Left field
This is actually the most fun comparison, because who do you like more, the 22-year-old power-and-defense superstar in Jackson Chourio -- the only player in history to have three 20-20 seasons through age-22 -- or the 25-year-old elite speed-and-contact guy in Chandler Simpson, who improved his defense to the point that both were named Gold Glove finalists last week? It’s yet another reminder that there’s more than one way to provide value, and certainly both teams are very pleased with their situations here. It’s hard, though, not to default to Chourio, who might already be a top-20 position player in the sport. If both can run and field, and only one has any power, then the advantage writes itself.
Advantage: Brewers
Center field
In Garrett Mitchell and Jonny DeLuca, you have two very strong defensive center fielders, though you’d probably give the slight edge here to DeLuca. (Cedric Mullins also carries a good glove, though this spot has belonged to DeLuca all month.) The question about their bats is what shape of production you prefer, in that Mitchell struck out considerably more than DeLuca, but he also had an on-base percentage 54 points higher, thanks in large part to a walk rate three times as high. While we’re not weighing postseason performance too much here, it’s worth noting that Mitchell has had some huge hits, while DeLuca mostly has not. This is about as razor-thin as we’ll see here, but even if Mitchell’s glove isn’t as good, it’s still good, and he gets on base. Edge, Milwaukee. A small one, anyway.
Advantage: Brewers
Right field
For everything that Sal Frelick has done for the Brewers over his four seasons with the team -- and he has done quite a bit -- this was not a terribly strong season for him, posting a career-worst 70 OPS+, and he’s managed only three singles and a few walks in the playoffs. That’s not to say that he can’t help the team win in other ways, because he can and does, but Tampa Bay’s Victor Mesa Jr. has been one of the team’s breakout stars, putting up not only a 127 OPS+ but also some truly elite defensive metrics, in just half a season. You’re already familiar, anyway, with his absolute cannon of a throwing arm. Mesa Jr. wasn’t on the Opening Day roster and didn’t even join the Rays for good until late May. He might just be one of the most important players in the World Series, though.
Advantage: Rays
Designated hitter
It would be hard to find two players who mean more to their respective teams than veterans Yandy Díaz (in his eighth season with Tampa Bay) and recently appointed Milwaukee captain Christian Yelich (in his ninth season as a Brewer). Neither plays the field much anymore, nor is either at or near their peak of offensive performance these days. But Díaz far outperformed Yelich during the regular season (124 OPS+ to 91 OPS+, where again, 100 is average), and that’s held true in the postseason, too, where Yelich has been held out of certain games against tough lefties in favor of Andrew Vaughn. At DH, literally the only thing that matters is “dangerous bat,” and that’s Díaz still, after all these years.
Advantage: Rays
Starting pitchers
If we’re talking about each team’s top three starters, which represent the bulk of a postseason rotation, then it’s Jacob Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and Robert Gasser for Milwaukee, and Drew Rasmussen, Freddy Peralta and Nick Martinez for Tampa Bay. Those six pitchers, so far in the playoffs, have combined for a 1.87 ERA. They’re not that good, obviously, with every underlying metric saying that the strikeout rate has been just average, and that they’ve been bailed out to some extent by excellent defense and relief pitching.
Still: When Misiorowski -- the presumptive NL Cy Young winner, the most dominant per-batter pitcher of the moment -- has the highest postseason ERA of these six, you know how strong each team is here. You really can’t look at full-season stats, either, because it goes without saying that the Tampa Bay version of Peralta is a very different pitcher than New York version we saw prior to the Trade Deadline. Misiorowski is the best of the six, but is he that much better than Rasmussen right now, himself an ace? Maybe not.
These are two strengths, but we like Tampa Bay ever so slightly more for one reason: depth. No Milwaukee starter, not even the top ones, has managed to get past five innings in the playoffs so far, which puts a lot of pressure on the bullpens. (There’s a particularly interesting angle here if Tampa Bay’s high-contact, flat-swing hitters can foul off enough Misiorowski pitches to wear him out, as has already happened to him this month.) If you look past the top three, you’d probably take Tampa Bay’s Griffin Jax and Ian Seymour to get outs a little more than Milwaukee’s Shane Drohan and Dustin May.
They’re both good, obviously. They’re World Series starting rotations. We’d give the ever-so-slight edge to Tampa Bay in a best of seven.
Advantage: Rays
Relief pitchers
If Milwaukee’s starters have been more good than great this month, then their relievers have more than picked up the slack, as you’ve almost certainly heard the note that in 40 2/3 postseason innings, the Brewers' bullpen has allowed all of six earned runs. While most of the focus there lands on Aaron Ashby or closer Trevor Megill, realize that JoJo Romero has a 47% strikeout rate this month, and that Abner Uribe, Antonio Senzatela, Megill and Ashby are all averaging more than 98 mph on their heaters this month. In fact, it is the second-hardest-throwing bullpen of the pitch tracking era (since 2008) -- at 98 mph even -- and the hardest that doesn’t include Mason Miller.
It makes, then, for an ironic matchup against a Tampa Bay bullpen that is A) also very good but B) does not throw hard, comparatively, at just 93.2 mph. (That goes down slightly, if you don't include Peralta’s impressive appearance in ALCS Game 4.) Much depends on the status of Bryan Baker, their All-Star closer, who was used so heavily against Cleveland that his fastball, which averaged 96.3 mph during the regular season, sunk below 93 mph in ALCS Game 6.
He was still good, of course. All the Rays are. It’s just hard not to go with Milwaukee, given their superior depth and full rest.
Advantage: Brewers
Prediction
It should be clear by now that this is an incredibly tightly matched series between two mirror-image teams, the best in their respective leagues, and you could as easily claim “rust or rest” for Milwaukee after their layoff, no matter which narrative you’d like to go with. Milwaukee has the biggest-name pitcher in Misiorowski; Tampa Bay has clearly the biggest star hitter in Caminero; and both sides play strong defense and win in ways that aren’t just waiting for the homer.
We like that Milwaukee has the home-field advantage, and the bullpen edge, and also that their lineup just seems a little deeper; in the second half of the season, no team -- not the Dodgers, not the Cubs, not anyone -- got more production from the No. 6 through 9 spots in their lineup than Milwaukee. That’s in part because of the middle infield, where the Brewers were third best, while Tampa Bay was third weakest. There’s at least some question about what shape Baker will be in, though three days of rest before the World Series ought to help.
It won’t be a cakewalk, because there’s too much talent and similarity on both sides for that. But every small edge matters, and Milwaukee has enough of them that we expect the second World Series title in city history, and the first for the Brewers franchise. Get ready to slide, Bernie.
Brewers in seven.

The Milwaukee Brewers' World Series roster should look almost exactly the same as it has so far this postseason.
Fresh off a dominant sweep in the NLCS against the back-to-back World Series champion Dodgers, the Brewers had a full week to prepare for this winner-take-all best-of-seven series.
Looking at the Rays lineup and how they construct things, it'll be interesting to see what Murphy goes with in the upcoming series.
Remember, Milwaukee has a pair of pitchers who have yet to pitch in the postseason despite being on the roster the entire time.
If there was ever a time for Big Woo to come back, it would be now, though the team must carefully weigh all of its options before pulling the trigger.

- David Hamilton

- Andrew Vaughn

- Jackson Chourio

Brewers make one roster change
When it comes to William Contreras and Gary Sanchez, neither of those players is going anywhere. Sanchez has yet to catch in the playoffs, and he likely won't, but he had a huge pinch-hit walk against Mason Miller in Game 2 of the NLDS.
Milwaukee will still carry six infielders and five outfielders. There isn't a world where they should mess with any of those 11 players. There are no injuries that have been made available to the public, and there's no one else who could fill those spots at this point in the year.
Pitching-wise, Chad Patrick has gotten loose a few times, so that's the only thing keeping him on the roster.
Woodruff shouldn't start a game unless it's at home and he's used as an opener. But, with where he's at, it certainly feels like he could give this team some useful bullpen innings, and there's no one more deserving to be on the roster than him.

item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays — the top team in the American League — has held its own to achieve the third pennant in franchise history, and their second this decade.
The Milwaukee Brewers are back in the World Series for the first time since 1982, and they're doing it as the National League's best team. The 103-win Crew swept the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS and now host the Tampa Bay Rays in a matchup of two franchise-first title seekers. Game 1 is Friday at American Family Field.
Here's a position-by-position look at the Brewers as they prepare for the Rays.
Catcher
William Contreras is the lead backstop for Milwaukee, and one of the most popular Brewers, as he has been one of the more reliable all-around catchers in the National League in recent years and in the playoffs, as his bat has stayed productive into October. He posted a strong 1.157 OPS with three homers through the NLCS while handling a staff that mixes elite velocity with a deep lefty presence.
At backup, the more familiar Gary Sánchez provides a power-oriented option off the bench.
Infield
The Brewers' infield blends elite defense, speed, and opportunistic offense.
- First base: Jake Bauers. The NLCS MVP has been the postseason story for Milwaukee. A well-known Rays prospect if you've read this site for any length of time, Bauers nearly retired but returned for what he considered one more season last year to keep his health insurance benefits after his wife became pregnant with their second child. Fast forward two seasons, and he has delivered lengthy at bats with power and timely hitting throughout October while providing solid enough defense at the corner. Veteran White Sox infielder Andrew Vaughn has also seen time at first and as a right-handed bat off the bench or at DH against lefties.
- Second base: Brice Turang. One of the best all-around second basemen in baseball and the No. 2 hitter. Turang combines Gold Glove-caliber defense with improved power (21 home runs and 100 RBIs in the regular season) and baserunning. He's a clear mismatch advantage and not to be trifled with.
- Shortstop: Cooper Pratt. The 22-year old rookie shortstop has started the bulk of the postseason games. He's shown a contact-oriented approach and improving glove work as the year has progressed, and pushing the previous starter Ortiz into a third base platoon.
- Third base: Joey Ortiz / David Hamilton. This has been a platoon/mix-and-match spot. The right handed hitting Ortiz and left handed hitting Hamilton now split time depending on matchups. If we are drawing comparisons, neither matches Junior Caminero's power, but both offer speed and defensive flexibility that fits Milwaukee's style.
Outfield
Milwaukee's outfield is built on athleticism, defense, and a rising star.
- Left field: Jackson Chourio. This 22-year-old superstar has continued his rapid ascent in 2026. Already with multiple 20-20 seasons under his belt, Chourio brings power, speed, and improving defense. He's the dynamic centerpiece of the lineup, their version of a Junior Caminero, and fun to watch.
- Center field: Garrett Mitchell. Strong defensive center fielder who has delivered several big hits in the playoffs, including a go-ahead home run in the NLCS clincher. He gets on base and covers ground.
- Right field: Sal Frelick. Elite defender with speed and contact skills. Luis Lara has spelled him against left-handers and provides another athletic option. The group ranks among the best defensive outfields in the league.
Technically also an outfielder, the Designated Hitter, Christian Yelich, remains in the lineup and was recently named club captain. While not at his peak production levels, his experience and ability to still impact games remain valuable, especially against right-handed pitching.
Rotation
Manager Pat Murphy has utilized short leashes and heavy bullpen support, but has a solid rotation heading into the World Series:
- Jacob Misiorowski — The clear ace and yet to be crowned NL Cy Young winner (16-5, 1.80 ERA, 252 strikeouts in the regular season). He's started Game 1 of both the NLDS and NLCS and will surely open the World Series. To say his high-velocity stuff that ranks among the best is an understatement. I half expected Misiorowski to mean fast in Polish, but apparently it's something closer to bear.
- Logan Henderson — The reliable No. 2. Solid second-half performer who has handled Game 2 duties effectively in his sophomore season as a homegrown talent.
- Robert Gasser — Emerged as the preferred Game 3 option after strong late-season form and solid postseason outings (including shutout work in the NLCS). He was acquired in the Josh Hader trade with San Diego, over came a UCL surgery in 2025, and started the year in Triple-A, making his rise a bit unexpected. His dad's best friend is evidently Vin Diesel.
- Dustin May (with Shane Drohan as an Opener) — May has postseason experience but has been used carefully; Florida State alumni Drohan opened Game 4 in the NLCS, and the southpaw seems likely to get the nod again given how well that went last time.
No starter has gone particularly deep in October, which is by design. Milwaukee trusts its relievers to take over after four or five innings, limiting any time-through-the-order penalties.
Bullpen
This unit has been the difference-maker. The Brewers' bullpen allowed just six earned runs across more than 40 postseason innings heading into the World Series and featured relievers earning the win in all four NLCS games during the sweep of Los Angeles.
- Trevor Megill — 6'8" Closer. Reliable late-inning presence, and a bit of an invention by the Brewers, having been added for a PTBNL in April 2023.
- Abner Uribe — Primary setup man. High-velocity right-hander who has been outstanding, despite blowing a save in Game 3 of the NLCS he's been their best bullpen arm this month.
- Aaron Ashby — Left-handed workhorse who has been nearly unhittable in October (multiple scoreless multi-inning outings) and got the save in Game 4 of the sweep.
- DL Hall / JoJo Romero — Additional lefty depth options that each were credited wins in the NLCS.
Regular season starter Kyle Harrison will likely find his way into the mix as well. The group throws exceptionally hard on average and enters the series fully rested after the NLCS sweep and the Rays' longer ALCS.
Conclusion
The Brewers' formula is clear: elite defense, contact and speed on offense, an electric frontline starter, and a lights-out bullpen that can cover the middle and late innings.
Against a similarly constructed Rays team that also emphasizes pitching, defense, and small-ball elements, the series should be tight, low-scoring, and decided by the margins. Milwaukee holds home-field advantage and the deeper, harder-throwing relief corps—two factors that could prove decisive in a first-time-champion showdown.

The Minnesota Twins have spent another October watching the postseason from home and the biggest question is why. The Twins have missed the playoffs in five of the past six seasons and while many are rightfully upset about the team’s payroll slashing, there are also several fundamental mistakes that have prevented them from being successful.
Those mistakes will be front and center during this year’s World Series. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the Fall Classic after completing a sweep over the Los Angeles Dodgers on Thursday night and they will face either the Tampa Bay Rays or Cleveland Guardians in what will be a showdown between small-market teams.
While this year’s matchup could create a loophole for the Pohlad family to avoid dropping a large amount of money to improve the team, it also reflects poorly on their decisions that have kept them from competing over the past few years.
The Brewers, Rays and Guardians are showing the Twins how to build a winner
As you may have guessed, the Brewers, Guardians and Rays are not among MLB’s biggest spenders. According to Cot’s Baseball Contracts, the Brewers’ year-end salary ranked 23rd at $99.3 million and defeated the Dodgers’ No. 1 roster at $366.0 million. The American League finalists were also budget-conscious as the Rays ranked 20th with a year-end payroll of $103.1 million and the Guardians ranked 25th at $91.0 million.
All three of the remaining teams had a lower year-end payroll than the Twins, who ranked 17th with a figure of $123.9 million and while many, including owner and chairman Tom Pohlad, believe that adding to that number could lead to a championship, the other three teams show what they have done wrong.
The first is maximizing the value of players on the roster. The Rays, Guardians and Brewers have traded players before they get to free agency to add to their organization and it’s paid off in a big way. The Brewers most notably did this in a February 2024 trade featuring Corbin Burnes that brought back left-hander DL Hall and infielder Joey Ortiz.
The Rays also have done this with their trade of Triple-A right-hander Tobias Myers, who was traded to Cleveland as he was eligible for the Rule 5 Draft in 2021, and brought back star third baseman Junior Caminero in return. While the Guardians whiffed on Myers, they made other shrewd deals that netted them Craig Yoho, Patrick Bailey, Foster Griffin and Kyle Manzardo.
These trades are a double-edged sword as they usually involve popular players. But it brings back pieces that ensure a larger championship window. That leaves player development as the final phase of the three contenders and each team has a homegrown star to lean on such as Jose Ramirez, Jacob Misiorowski or Caminero.
The Twins’ biggest problems go beyond their payroll
Turning the attention back to the Twins, it’s easy to see where they have come up short. This year’s trade deadline was one opportunity to shift the narrative. But instead of trading players that could bring back a big return such as Ryan Jeffers and Joe Ryan, the Twins went the opposite direction, adding A.J. Minter, Jeff Hoffman and Dean Kremer.
Even when they tried to trade Trevor Larnach to the Houston Astros before owner Jim Crane vetoed it, they were seeking 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, a pitcher who posted his highest ERA (3.73) and lowest WAR (1.0) since his rookie season in 2021.
The other key issue is the Twins’ player development. While top prospects such as Royce Lewis and Matt Wallner thrive initially when reaching the major leagues, those players have hit a wall when pitchers adjust to them. The problem can be traced back to Miguel Sano’s downfall in the early 2020s and can still be seen in a group of post-hype hitters that haven’t lived up to their prospect status.
This leaves the Twins in a tricky spot this offseason. After failing to trade Jeffers at the deadline, there’s a good chance he’ll leave in free agency. Ryan has a year of team control remaining, but trading him now could get a pair of MLB-ready players in return. Several top prospects including Walker Jenkins, Emmanuel Rodriguez and Kaelen Culpepper made their debuts this season, but the key will be to make sure they don’t regress entering their first full season in the bigs.
Of course, fans may cheer for a salary floor to hold the Pohlads accountable for what happens to the Twins next. But the Rays, Guardians and Brewers show that paying top dollar may not be necessary to build a contender and Minnesota would be wise to follow their blueprint.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- Jake Bauers put his team’s determination on full display, getting the Milwaukee Brewers within one victory of their first World Series appearance in 44 years.
Bauers turned an 11-pitch at-bat into a go-ahead two-run homer in the seventh inning as the Brewers took a commanding 3-0 lead in the National League Championship Series with a 6-2 victory Wednesday night against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Milwaukee will aim for a sweep of the best-of-7 series tonight at Dodger Stadium.
Garrett Mitchell followed Bauers with a homer of his own as the Southern California natives put on a show in front of family and friends in a ballpark where the home team has played the bully for more than a decade.
“We play for each other. It’s as simple as that, man,” Bauers said. “Any time there’s a mistake, an error, a walk, pitchers give up runs, hitters strike out in a big spot, the only thing anybody’s thinking about is how can I help pick that guy up? How can I help pick that guy up and do my part to win this game?”
Rookie left-hander Robert Gasser gave up three hits over five scoreless innings as the Brewers moved closer to the franchise’s second trip to the World Series. The Brewers made their lone Fall Classic appearance in 1982 as an American League team, losing in seven games to the St. Louis Cardinals.
Jackson Chourio led off the game with a first-pitch homer off Dodgers left-hander Blake Snell as Milwaukee showed its power capabilities after finishing last in the National League in homers during the regular season with 154.
“Job’s not finished yet,” Mitchell said. “Just got to take it a day at a time, not really worried about what’s happened today, what happened yesterday or what’s coming tomorrow. We’ve just got to show up and continue to play our brand of baseball and continue doing it for one another.”
Will Smith hit a two-run double for the Dodgers, who won the past two World Series titles. Los Angeles is trying to become the first National League club to win three consecutive Fall Classic championships.
Los Angeles manager Dave Roberts moved Shohei Ohtani to sixth in the batting order with the superstar in a postseason slump. Ohtani went 1-for-2 with a walk and a hit-by-pitch. The Dodgers’ offense was held to five hits in Game 3 after collecting three in Game 2.
“I haven’t digested this one,” Roberts said when asked about potential lineup changes for Game 4. “They’re going to run a bullpen game. Just trying to figure out which guys we want to be in there, how you kind of construct the lineup, but I haven’t thought about that one yet.”
Snell appeared to recover from Chourio’s ambush home run before he was rocked by consecutive home runs with no outs in the seventh. Snell (0-1) allowed four runs on four hits in six-plus innings with two walks and nine strikeouts.
“I just left the fastball over the middle to Bauers,” said Snell, who was in the Tampa Bay Rays organization with Bauers from 2015-18. “… I’ve seen the ups and downs he’s been through, and it’s been a lot of downs. So for him to go through this right now, he’s earned it. Hats off to him. What an at-bat.”
Trailing 1-0 from the jump, the Dodgers managed to put their leadoff batter on base in four of the first six innings before finally breaking through.
Gasser was replaced by right-hander Abner Uribe to open the sixth inning, and the reliever walked three of the first four batters he faced to load the bases, including a walk to Ohtani. Smith delivered a double off the wall in left-center field for a 2-1 lead after entering the game in a 1-for-25 slump.
Los Angeles failed to add onto the lead in the inning against left-hander DL Hall (3-0) when Enrique Hernandez and Tommy Edman struck out to end the threat.
Milwaukee responded immediately when Andrew Vaughn walked to open the seventh before Bauers’ epic at-bat. Two pitches later, Mitchell went over the wall in right-center field for a 4-2 advantage to end Snell’s outing.
Bauers had a similar plate appearance in Game 2 when he worked a 12-pitch walk with two outs in the third inning and Christian Yelich followed with a two-run single.
“Yeah, there was for sure a moment where I thought to myself like, ‘Oh, you’re in it again,’” Bauers said. “As far as the approach for the at-bat, I didn’t want to miss a fastball.”
The Brewers added to their lead in the eighth when Brice Turang scored on a Justin Wrobleski wild pitch, and Joey Ortiz tacked on an RBI single in the ninth.
Hall threw 2⅓ scoreless innings. Brewers closer Trevor Megill got the last four outs, striking out the final two batters, for his fourth save of the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES – Pat Murphy clearly had bigger fish to fry on Wednesday, Oct. 14 with his Milwaukee Brewers preparing to face the Los Angeles Dodgers in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series at Dodger Stadium.
But there was some Brewers-adjacent news that broke earlier in the day that irked Murphy – one of his best players had seemingly been disrespected.
William Contreras, whose 1,085 ⅔ innings and 9.064 pitches caught led the major leagues, was not among the three finalists at catcher in the National League for the Rawlings Gold Glove Award.
Those catchers were Freddy Fermin of the San Diego Padres, Gabriel Moreno of the Arizona Diamondbacks and Luis Torrens of the New York Mets.
"Contreras, he wasn't in there? Contreras?" said Murphy when asked initially for his reaction both to Brice Turang and Jackson Chourio being named finalists at second base and in left field, respectively, as well as any Brewers players he thought might have been snubbed.
"I'm biased. I get to see him 100-plus games catching. I think he caught the most games in the major leagues this year, and he was so important to us. They should come up with another award for William, because he's been incredible.
"So, if he's not on that list, ask for a redo."
The criteria is listed by Rawlings as the following:
To determine the winners of the 18 defensive position Awards, each team's manager and up to six coaches on his staff vote from a pool of qualified players in their League and cannot vote for players from their own team. In 2013, Rawlings added the SABR Defensive Index™ (SDI) to the Rawlings Gold Glove Award selection process, which comprises approximately 25 percent of the overall selection total, with the managers' and coaches' votes continuing to carry the majority.
To identify the utility Award winners, Rawlings collaborated with the Society for American Baseball Research (SABR) to create a specialized defensive formula separate from the traditional selection process for the Rawlings Gold Glove Award position winners. Utilizing the SABR formula and additional defensive statistics, Rawlings will select one utility winner from each League.
Looking at metrics, Contreras did rate out poorly in areas like framing (minus-6, 53rd out of 56 qualified catchers) and blocks above average (minus-7 on 4,361 opportunities). But with Contreras behind the plate, Brewers pitchers threw to a 3.32 ERA with the team ultimately going 80-41.
Contreras also threw out 28.4% of would-be basestealers (19 of 67).
Joey Ortiz also failed to make the cut as a utility player despite finishing 15th in the major leagues with 15 outs above average and also logged eight total defensive runs saved between third base and shortstop.
"Joey's a great defender," said Murphy. "I don't know the other guys in the league, but Joey, if given the chance to play every day on a team, you'd be hard-pressed to find a better defender. I don't know how all the voting takes place and everything. I know I vote, but I don't remember who was on there and who wasn't. You can't vote for your own players anyway.
"I try to just really vote for who I think is the best. I think you're doing a disservice if you try to like, 'Well, I don't want to vote for this guy because my guy's in competition.' I just voted for the guys that I think are the best. But for Contreras not to be on there, I don't know what it's based on. There's so many things in the catching position that you can't measure.
"So, now I'm kind of ticked about it now that you brought it up."

The Baltimore Orioles have some serious work to do this offseason.
After entering this season with high expectations, they underperformed immensely. The Orioles finished the season with a 79-82 record and fourth in the AL East.
With how this campaign went, the Orioles should look to make multiple additions to their roster this offseason. One specific area that they should aim to improve is their infield.
Due to this, the Orioles are now being urged to trade for one of their former infielders from the Milwaukee Brewers.
Baltimore Orioles Urged to Trade for Brewers’ Joey Ortiz
In a recent article for Sports Illustrated, Jason La Canfora urged the Orioles to bring back infielder Joey Ortiz this offseason through trade.
“Ortiz, part of Baltimore’s package to land Corbin Burnes, is a whiz with the glove – elite, elite. plenty athletic and they need a lefty bat somewhere in this infield mix (especially if Henderson and/or Holliday go) and he is fresh only playing about 500 innings a year at short at the Brewers move him around,” La Canfora wrote.
The idea of the Orioles bringing back Ortiz is an interesting one. He is a player who the Orioles are already familiar with, so he could be worth acquiring again to strengthen their roster.
Ortiz had a strong regular season for the Brewers in 2026. In 134 games this campaign, he posted nine home runs, 47 RBI, and a .270 batting average. This was after he had seven home runs, 45 RBI, and a .230 batting average in 2025. With this, Ortiz took a step forward with his play this campaign. Thus, he could be worth reuniting with for the Orioles.
Looking Back at Ortiz’s Time With the Orioles
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS – SEPTEMBER 02: Joey Ortiz #3 of the Milwaukee Brewers hits a two-RBI single during the ninth inning against the Chicago Cubs at Wrigley Field on September 02, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images)
Ortiz was selected by the Orioles in the fourth round of the 2019 MLB Draft, 108th overall. From there, he played his first season with the Orioles in 2023.
In 15 games for the Orioles during the 2023 season, he recorded one double, four RBI, and a .212 batting average in 15 games. This would mark the end of Ortiz’s time with the Orioles, though. This is because he was traded to the Brewers ahead of the 2024 season.
Overall, Ortiz’s time with the Orioles was brief. However, with the Orioles needing another reliable infielder, it would make sense if they tried to bring him back. He has found success with the Brewers and could improve Baltimore’s roster. Furthermore, when noting that he is in the early stages of his career, he still could get even better.
Nevertheless, it will be interesting to see if the Orioles pursue Ortiz during this offseason. The fit looks good on paper.

The Milwaukee Brewers have an unfortunate history of late-season injuries preceding postseason runs. September injuries to Christian Yelich and Brandon Woodruff are the most recent examples, but the trend also extends to Devin Williams breaking his hand after punching a wall in 2021, Ben Sheets not being a part of the 2008 postseason run after a flexor tendon injury, and of course, Rollie Fingers' forearm injury ahead of the team's memorable 1982 run.
With just over 24 hours remaining until the Brewers' 2026 postseason opener, this year's team thankfully hasn't made a contribution to that disheartening list. However, as the Brewers finish out their stretch of five days off -- the result of them earning a first-round bye -- there was an injury scare that had Brewers fans feeling déjà vu.
Infielder Joey Ortiz exited the Brewers' Friday night opener in their final series of the regular season with a noticeable limp. After the game, manager Pat Murphy revealed that Ortiz had been battling soreness in his knee due to a bruise he sustained during the team's series against the Philadelphia Phillies and also some inflammation in his abdomen that has been causing him discomfort.
Ortiz didn't play either of the final two games of the regular season, and his postseason roster status was briefly in doubt when Murphy couldn't commit one way or another on Tuesday afternoon. However, thankfully, during Friday's media availability, the Brewers' manager took a more optimistic tone when talking about his injured infielder. Said Murphy on Ortiz on Friday afternoon, "It looks like it's progressing in the right direction...I would say at this point we're planning on him being available."
The Brewers are planning on Joey Ortiz "being available" for the NLDS
Despite his struggles during the 2025 season and first half of the 2026 campaign, Ortiz became one of the Brewers' most productive hitters during the second half of this year. In fact, Ortiz had the ninth best OPS (.883) among NL hitters with at least 200 plate appearances, from July 1 to the end of the season. As crazy as the statement would have sounded during the middle of May, Ortiz is one of the Brewers' key offensive X-factors heading into the postseason.
Therefore, it would have been a significant blow had Ortiz missed out on the 2026 postseason run due to his late-season knee and abdomen injuries, but thankfully the Brewers' infielder is expected to be available tomorrow night.
Ortiz's production would indicate that he should start every game regardless of the handedness of the opposing pitcher, but Murphy consistently used David Hamilton against tough right-handed starters at third base, so it's not yet certain just how many games Joey O will start in the postseason. That said, the Padres just announced that southpaw Robbie Ray is getting the ball in Game 1, so Ortiz will almost certainly be manning the hot corner on Saturday night. Regardless of how many at-bats Murphy gives his surging third baseman in October, it's undeniably a welcome development that Ortiz will likely be available for the NLDS roster.

The Milwaukee Brewers don't have to reveal their National League Division Series roster until Saturday morning, but the organization gave a positive update on Friday ahead of the official announcement.
Throughout the week, the guy to watch from an injury perspective has been infielder Joey Ortiz. The 28-year-old has been dealing with knee and abdominal injuries, but is trending in the right direction. Brewers manager Pat Murphy said so himself on Friday and noted that the expectation is that he will be good to go for the National League Division Series.
"It looks like it's progressing in the right direction," Murphy said. "He's still ... he still has some pain. He's going to tell you, 'no,' and all that kind of stuff. He wants to play very badly. I would say at this point, we are planning on him being available."
Joey Ortiz Is Going To Be Alright
There was a point during the 2026 season in which this update wouldn't have moved the needle much for Milwaukee. But things are certainly different now. Before he shifted from shortstop to third base, Ortiz was really struggling offensively. He was batting .207 with one home run and 14 RBIs in 60 games before Cooper Pratt made his big league debut. Pratt made his debut on June 16, which shifted Ortiz's role away from shortstop.
Things changed for the better for Ortiz afterward. From June 17 through the end of the season, Ortiz slashed .310/.348/.491 with an .840 OPS, eight home runs, 33 RBIs, nine doubles and four triples in 74 games.
He went from being someone at risk of being sent down to the minors, to being integral to this club's success down the stretch. Fortunately, when the Brewers open up National League Division Series play on Saturday, the current expectation is that Ortiz will be in the mix, barring some sort of last-second setback.
The Brewers have a tough series ahead. The San Diego Padres are the hottest team in baseball and aren't going to be an easy out. For the Brewers to win, they're going to need all of the help that they can get. So, this update is very positive for the organization heading into their most important series of the season so far. If the Brewers can take down the Padres in the NLDS, they would advance to face either the Los Angeles Dodgers or the Atlanta Braves in the National League Championship Series.

Brewers record their first 100-win season with victory over Phillies
The Milwaukee Brewers reached 100 wins for the first time, and Jackson Chourio hit his 25th homer to lift them to a 5-1 victory over Philadelphia on Thursday night that slowed the Phillies’ playoff push.
The Phillies needed a win to at least have a shot at clinching their fifth straight trip to the playoffs. They instead can try again to clinch for the third straight game on Friday against Tampa Bay.
Philadelphia played without NL batting leader Luis Arraez after he came off with a sprained left ankle after he tried to avoid a tag at first base.
Milwaukee reached one more milestone to go with its National League Central title and a first-round postseason bye. The Brewers are the first team this year to reach 100 wins and are trying to hold off the defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers for the No. 1 seed in the NL playoffs. Their previous high was 97 wins last year.
Brewers fans crowded the seats behind the dugout and held “100” signs as players left the field.
Bryce Harper tied the game 1-1 with an RBI single in the third.
Jake Bauers hit the tie-breaking single off José Alvarado (5-4) in the eighth inning, and Cooper Pratt and Joey Ortiz added run-scoring singles in the inning for a 4-1 lead. Chourio hit a solo shot in the ninth.
JoJo Romero (3-3) got the win and Antonio Senzatela earned his fourth save.
Phillies starter Andrew Painter had another terrific outing in a second-half rebound that should see him play a role in the postseason in the rotation or out of the bullpen. He allowed Sam Frelick’s RBI double in the second and finished with eight strikeouts and three walks in six innings.
The rookie right-hander was demoted to the minors in June after a 12-4 loss to Miami left him with eight losses in nine decisions and a 7.06 ERA. Since his July 31 recalled has a 3.65 ERA in 11 starts with 62 strikeouts to 23 walks.
Philadelphia got more good pitching news earlier in the day when All-Star lefty Jesús Luzardo said he has recovered enough from left shoulder inflammation that he should be able to pitch next week in the playoffs.
Up next
Milwaukee tunes up for the playoffs with a three-game homestand against St. Louis.

Brewers take down Phillies for franchise's first 100-win season
(Photo credit: Bill Streicher)
Jake Bauers' RBI single in the eighth inning plated the go-ahead run Thursday for the Milwaukee Brewers, who reached the 100-win mark for the first time in franchise history with their 5-1 win over the hosting Philadelphia Phillies.
Bauers, who went 2-for-5 and added a double, singled up the middle, allowing Jackson Chourio to score from second, giving the Brewers (100-59) a 2-1 lead and starting a three-run frame. Chourio, who pinch-hit for designated hitter William Contreras, led off the frame with a walk off Jose Alvarado (5-4) and stole second.
Gary Sanchez singled deep to left field to put runners on the corners, and after Alvarado got Luis Lara to line out to shallow center, Cooper Pratt (2-for-3) welcomed Chase Shugart with another hit up the middle to give the Brewers a two-run lead. Joey Ortiz added a two-out hit, a blooper to shallow center that allowed Sanchez to score from second.
Chourio added a solo home run, his 25th blast of the season, in the ninth.
Five Brewers pitchers held the Phillies (87-72) to just four hits. JoJo Romero (3-3) allowed one hit in 1 1/3 innings against St. Louis, who Milwaukee acquired him from last month. Romero picked up his second win with the Brewers since coming off the injured list (appendectomy) earlier this month.
Antonio Senzatela relieved Romero, allowing a walk over the final 1 2/3 innings to earn his fourth save.
Phillies starter Andrew Painter held the Brewers to just one run over six innings. The rookie allowed five hits and three walks while matching a season-high eight strikeouts. His only blemish came in the second, when Sal Frelick doubled home Sanchez.
Kyle Schwarber (2-for-4) and Bryce Harper (2-for-4) combined to get all four of the Phillies hits. Harper's third-inning single scored Schwarber, who led off the frame with a double off Brewers starter Shane Drohan. Philadelphia managed just one hit, a Schwarber single in the seventh, against the Brewers bullpen.
Besides losing the game, the Phillies may also have lost infielder Luis Arraez, who reportedly sprained an ankle trying to avoid a tag on a groundout in the sixth inning.
With the win, Milwaukee can officially clinch home-field advantage throughout the postseason should the Los Angeles Dodgers lose Thursday night to the visiting San Diego Padres.
Philadelphia remains in an NL wild-card spot, but the Phillies could not drop their magic number to clinch from two.
--Field Level Media

When the Milwaukee Brewers faced off against the Philadelphia Phillies on Tuesday night, they didn't have third baseman Joey Ortiz in the lineup.
Ortiz is someone who has had a roller coaster of a season, to say the least. He spent the first few months at shortstop and was very good defensively, but really struggled offensively. At the time, it was talked about how Cooper Pratt would be coming at some point and that would be bad news for Ortiz's role. When Pratt did arrive, Ortiz moved to third base. At the time, his bat also came alive.
He has turned his season around and he has become a key cog in this lineup, which at one point was very unexpected. But he wasn't in the lineup on Tuesday against the righty Zack Wheeler. Is that something Brewers fans should expect in the playoffs? Brewers manager Pat Murphy broke down that very question, as shared on X by MLB.com's Adam McCalvy.
"Joey doesn't work as well versus that two-seamer, but if it was the playoffs today, Joey would be in there," Murphy said. "He's been so good for us, and I don't want to waver his confidence at all. But he's got a little abdominal strain thing going on that he's been fighting. I noticed a little bit of it a couple of days ago. We're looking to get him a break. And we need to get [David Hamilton] in there. Same with [Luis Lara]. I would probably start [Sal Frelick] today, but we have to get Lara some at-bats against right-handers, too."
Joey Ortiz Will Help Milwaukee
This is an intriguing insight into how the club is viewing the playoff lineup already. Earlier in the season, there was more of a committee at third base. Ortiz and Hamilton both got a chunk of time, but Ortiz really has turned around his season to the point that he deserves to be the main guy.
Ortiz has played in 131 games so far this season and is slashing .267/.326/.403 with a .729 OPS, nine home runs, 46 RBIs, nine stolen bases, 14 doubles, four triples and 49 runs scored. Plus, on top of his elite defense, he doesn't strike out. Ortiz has struck out just 78 times in his 131 games played.
When it comes to the Phillies, they are realistically a team Milwaukee could face in the National League Division Series. If the season were to end today, the Phillies would face the Chicago Cubs in the Wild Card round with the winner of the three-game series heading to face Milwaukee.
If the Brewers and the Phillies face off in the playoffs, Milwaukee will very likely see Wheeler again and it sounds like the lineup would look different, especially with Ortiz. Murphy noted that he would probably start Sal Frelick in a playoff game in this scenario as well.
It may have just been a regular season game on a Tuesday. But we did get some valuable insights into how this club is viewing the lineup heading into the postseason.

A falta de una semana para que termine la temporada regular en la MLB, el panorama de playoffs comienza a definirse y con ello te presentamos aquellos peloteros mexicanos que ya aseguraron su clasificación a playoffs y quienes todavía están en la pelea por entrar a la postemporada.
Mexicanos que ya aseguraron su pase a postemporada
La presencia de peloteros mexicanos en las últimas ediciones de los playoffs ha sido constante y este año no será la excepción pues hasta ahorita se tiene confirmada la participación de cuatro peloteros mexicanos y dos con estatus todavía pendiente, ya que uno está en sucursales y el otro se encuentra en lista de lesionados.
PUBLICIDAD
A continuación, te presentamos la lista de jugadores nacionales que estarán en los playoffs:
Jonathan Aranda (Tampa Bay Rays)
Ha firmado su campaña más sólida y consagratoria en MLB. Con 149 juegos jugados, el infielder presume un promedio de bateo de .277, conectando 156 imparables, 22 cuadrangulares y remolcando 92 carreras, convirtiéndose en una pieza medular en el lineup de los Rays.
Jarren Durán (Boston Red Sox):
Se ha consolidado como un auténtico motor en los senderos y el jardín central. A lo largo de la temporada suma 20 jonrones, 69 carreras impulsadas y 19 bases robadas en 145 encuentros, destacando además por su velocidad con 5 triples.

Joey Ortiz (Milwaukee Brewers):
Ha sido una de las grandes revelaciones del año tras su llegada a Milwaukee, aportando una defensa de élite en el cuadro y un bateo sumamente oportuno que ayudó a los Brewers a amarrar temprano su boleto a octubre.
Patrick Sandoval (Boston Red Sox):
El lanzador que representó a México en el Clásico Mundial de Beisbol regresó esta temporada tras un periodo largo fuera de las canchas y ha tenido altibajos con los Boston Red Sox con una efectividad de 5.15 y un récord de 1-7.
Manuel Rodríguez (Tampa Bay Rays):
El lanzador yucateco venía sumando valiosos relevos con efectividad de 3.86 y 8 ponches en el bullpen de Tampa Bay en los cuatro juegos que disputó.

Alek Thomas (Oklahoma City Comets):
Después de haber sido cambiado desde los Arizona Diamondbacks a inicios de año, el jardinero Alek Thomas se encuentra actualmente en las sucursales de Los Angeles Dodgers
Aunque tuvo una breve participación de 7 juegos con el primer equipo de los Dodgers bateando para .211, la tremenda profundidad del roster angelino ha hecho que se mantenga buscando ritmo en el sistema de ligas menores, a la espera de un llamado que lo devuelva al roster de postemporada.

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees’ odds of winning the AL East are down to 2.8 percent per FanGraphs after getting walked off by the Diamondbacks last night. I know mathematically that makes sense, but the chances mentally feel even more extreme. I’ve been having “fun” (or whatever) comping the odds to certain pitchers from history getting a hit. We are the dregs. Remember mid-2000s Mets pitcher Aaron Heilman? I personally remember him most for giving up the homer to Yadier Molina late in Game 7 of the 2006 NLCS, just before Adam Wainwright famously caught Carlos Beltrán looking to win the pennant.
Anyway, Heilman was a horrendous hitter. He singled once in his rookie year, and then never got another hit. He ended his career 1-for-47, so an .021 average. So the Yankees just need magic only a little bit more sufficient than that RBI single by Heilman off Sidney Ponson on August 12, 2003! Hell yeah.
It’s not happening, but we press on because it’s good to check up on what everyone else is doing anyway. Here’s what was going on Saturday.
Tampa Bay Rays (94-60) 2, Boston Red Sox (84-71) 1
The Yankees gained a full game on the Rays on Friday for the first time in over a week, as Boston snapped their six-game winning streak. There was no such fortune to be found yesterday though; Tampa Bay made sure of that well before first pitch in Arizona, and it only got worse from there. By the end of the night, the Rays once again had a five-game lead over the Yanks; Tampa Bay’s magic number (combination of Rays wins or Yankees losses) to clinch the AL East is four.
This one was a pitchers’ duel to the bitter end. Brayan Bello had easily his best outing of a turbulent season (and probably the best of his career), firing eight shutout frames at the Trop and fanning 11 Rays, tying a personal best from July 9, 2024. As he only went 5.1 in that one and faced merely the soon-to-depart-Oakland A’s rather than the division-leading Rays.
The only true blemish on Bello’s record came when Jonathan Aranda cracked an opposite-field homer to make it a 1-1 game in the fourth. Tampa Bay had a chance to make it 2-1 against Bello in the seventh when Liam Hicks and Chandler Simpson led off with singles. Bello then induced a grounder from Victor Mesa Jr. to move up the runners, and then another off the bat of Richie Palacios to Trevor Story, who nailed pinch-runner Jonny DeLuca at home. Palacios swiped second, but Bello fanned Cedric Mullins to end the inning. The Rays went down in order in the eighth to end Bello’s brilliant night.
Unfortunately for Bello, a win wasn’t in the cards because Boston put up next to nothing against Freddy Peralta and the Rays’ pitching staff. Doubles by Caleb Durbin and Roman Anthony gave the Red Sox their one run in the second, but they were stymied from there. They had chances!
- Second inning after Anthony’s two-out double: Mickey Gasper lineout to center
- Fourth inning with runners on first and second, one out: Story strikeout, Durbin popout
- Fifth inning with runner on second, one out: Anthony groundout, Gasper strikeout
- Sixth inning with runners on first and second, two out: Durbin fly out to left
- Eighth inning after Adley Rutschman’s one-out double: Wilyer Abreu strikeout, Nick Sogard lineout
Even against lockdown Rays closer Bryan Baker, Boston had one last shot to take a late lead. After Story grounded out, Durbin lined a double down the left field line to put himself in scoring position for Jarren Duran. Durbin darted from second, however, and got thrown out stealing third. Duran promptly followed with a triple over DeLuca’s head in center. Isiah Kiner-Falefa bounced one to Junior Caminero at third to end the threat.
Granted a chance to walk it off, Tampa Bay didn’t waste it. Rather than blasting a homer to finish the game as he had twice earlier this homestand, Caminero began the ninth against Garrett Whitlock with a single to left. (A catwalk curtailed Durbin’s effort to catch a popup earlier in the AB.) DeLuca popped up, but Chandler Simpson grounded one through the six-hole for another hit. The runners moved up when catcher Connor Wong let a Whitlock sinker up bounce off his glove for a passed ball. Palacios ended the night with flare to center that fell in, securing the win for Tampa Bay. At least the Wild Card Series is also almost certainly going to be at Yankee Stadium now, I suppose.
AL Rock Fight
Cleveland Guardians (80-75) 12, The Athletics (61-94) 6
Two crooked numbers effectively decided Saturday’s affair with the A’s in a hurry. Tanner Bibee kind of stunk and would allow six runs in a dozen hits while failing to make through five, but it hardly mattered. Cleveland erased a 2-0 deficit in the first on a three-run shot from rookie Chase DeLauter and two-run homer by Angel Martinez. The A’s got one back in the third, only to see another five-spot from the Guardians on poor Jacob Lopez as David Fry, Austin Hedges, and Brayan Rocchio all delivered RBI doubles. Martinez later added a homer and an RBI single in a career-best four-hit day.
Chicago White Sox (79-76) 3, Detroit Tigers (73-82) 1
Cleveland’s win meant that Chicago was stuck at a game back in the AL Central in the best-case, but they did at least help push one of their Wild Card foes out of the picture with a win. Honestly, this was probably kind of a dud of a game for anyone who isn’t a White Sox fan, the lone highlights being Sean Burke’s six scoreless frames and Miguel Vargas’ sixth-inning solo shot to make it 3-1, Chicago (the other runs scored on an RBI single by Munetaka Murakami and a fifth-inning sac fly). Spencer Torkelson had a chance to tie the game with a homer following Hao-Yu Lee’s two-out single in the ninth, but he flew out to center to end it.
Milwaukee Brewers (97-58) 1, Baltimore Orioles (75-80) 0
Yeah, it’s time to stick a fork in the O’s. It was all but certain for awhile now, but Chicago’s win combined with Baltimore’s second-straight loss to Milwaukee means that the Orioles are four back with a week to play, plus multiple teams in front of them. Trevor Rogers was the hard-luck loser here while Baltimore got blanked on four hits and Rece Hinds lost a fly ball from Joey Ortiz in the sun, allowing him to triple and score on Gary Sánchez’s RBI grounder. Woof.
Texas Rangers (78-77) 6, Toronto Blue Jays (76-79) 1
The O’s aren’t the only bird that are all but shot down, either. Trade Deadline acquisition José Soriano coughed up an early homer to Josh Jung, beginning a five-inning, six-run outing that pushed Toronto three games out in the Wild Card and the Rangers into a one-game AL West lead over Houston. The only downside for Texas was that second-half surprise Cal Quantrill—who has a 1.75 ERA since re-entering the rotation in late July—left in the second with lat tightness, so old friend Jordan Montgomery picked up the slack in long relief, retiring 11 of the 12 hitters he faced with no hits allowed.
Atlanta Braves (91-64) 6, Houston Astros (77-78) 3
Houston and Texas have been wrestling all week over the prestigious “Who can win this horri-awful division with a .500-ish record” crown. Sunday it went to Texas with the Astros falling out of their tie for first place (remember that they own the tiebreaker). Isaac Paredes had put Houston ahead with a solo homer and an RBI knock in the third, but the Astros’ bullpen set that lead on fire. The big blow came off the bat of Ronald Acuña Jr., who belted a grand slam off Bryan Abreu in the seventh after AJ Blubaugh made a right mess of things.

BALTIMORE (AP) — The Milwaukee Brewers tied a team record with their 97th win of the season, beating Baltimore 1-0 Saturday with the help of a fly ball lost in the sun by Orioles right fielder Rece Hinds.
Already assured of their fourth straight NL Central title and eighth playoff berth in nine season, the big league-best Brewers (97-58) matched the wins total of last year’s team that finished 97-65.
Baltimore (75-80) fell four games behind the Chicago White Sox for the AL’s last wild card with seven to play.
Robert Gasser (5-5) allowed three hits over seven innings, Abner Uribe worked around a leadoff single in the eighth, and Aaron Ashby pitched a perfect ninth for his third save, finishing the Brewers’ 11th shutout this season and first 1-0 win.
Hinds lost Joey Ortiz’s fly ball in the sun in the second inning and tumbled to the ground, and Gary Sánchez hit into a run-scoring groundout.
Trevor Rogers (10-11) struck out 10, walked one and allowed three hits in a season-high eight innings.
Up next
Milwaukee RHP Jacob Misiorowski (15-5, 1.89 ERA) faces Baltimore RHP Brandon Young (9-4, 3.65) as the three-game series concludes Sunday night.

The Milwaukee Brewers are nearing the end of the MLB regular season. They defeated the Baltimore Orioles 6-5 Friday night, with Jackson Chourio driving in three runs. Prior to Game 2, the team announced news regarding Christian Yelich.
Saturday's game will feature a pitching battle between Robert Gasser and Trevor Rogers. The game will be broadcast at 3:05 PM Central Time, 4:05 PM Eastern Time. The Brewers are 8-2 in their last 10 contests, while the Orioles are 6-4.
Milwaukee Brewers Announce Big Christian Yelich News During Baltimore Orioles Series
Prior to the first pitch of their second game against the Orioles, the Brewers announced lineup news. For Yelich fans, the news is especially important.
- LF: Jackson Chourio
- 1B: Vaughn
- C: Gary Sanchez
- SS: Cooper Pratt
- RF: Luis Lara
- 2B: David Hamilton
Starting Pitcher: Robert Gasser.
Judging from the roster for today's game, Gary Sanchez is coming in while Yelich comes out. William Contreras moves to designated hitter to make room for Sanchez.
Yelich is a 34-year-old slugger, while Sanchez is a 33-year-old catcher for the Brewers.
Looking At Christian Yelich & Gary Sanchez
Yelich is a 14-year MLB veteran who has been with the Brewers for nine seasons.
Over his career, he has been an All-Star several times, culminating in an NL MVP award in 2018. Yelich has enjoyed a solid 2026 campaign, notching 101 hits, 57 RBIs, 11 stolen bases, and 11 home runs in 112 games.
On the other hand, Sanchez has 44 hits, 35 RBIs, and 11 home runs in 83 games.
Pat Murphy on Christian Yelich
Recently, the Brewers manager has discussed Yelich's work ethic and his dedication to the game.
"I just remember he was here one night till 1 o'clock in the morning. A lot of guys in his situation, you've won MVP, you've been an all-star multiple times, you've done all the things in the game, you are 12 years in your career, and you know what: he still cares so much about the Milwaukee Brewers. That's the beauty of this whole thing…you have no idea how much this guy cares," Murphy said via a social media clip from Hunter Baumgardt.

Whether Yelich is in the lineup or taking a night off to stay healthy for a deep playoff run, it sounds like Brewers fans are lucky to have him.
